No need to drop rice: a katori of cooked rice and two rotis land in about the same calories, roughly 150 to 200 kcal. What moves fat loss is the total for the day, so keep rice to one katori and fill the rest of the plate with dal, sabzi and curd. Your weight is coming down on pace with rice in the picture, from 84.2 to 81.9 kg.

A katori of cooked dal gives about 7 to 9 g protein, along with a fair amount of carbs, so it helps but won't carry 120 g on its own. Pair it with a denser source at each meal: 100 g paneer or tofu, a katori of soya chunks, or a bowl of curd. Today you're at 28 g, so two meals like that would close most of the gap.
100 g of paneer has about 18 to 20 g protein, but also around 20 g fat and 260 to 300 kcal. Low-fat paneer or tofu gives similar protein for fewer calories if you want more room.
Ghee doesn't burn fat; it's pure fat at about 45 kcal per teaspoon, so it adds up quickly. A teaspoon or two a day on dal or roti is fine and fits your 1800 kcal. Just measure it rather than pouring.

Not really for weight: jaggery has about the same calories as sugar, around 20 kcal a teaspoon, and the extra iron or minerals are tiny at that amount. If the chai is a daily habit, cutting the sweetener down gradually helps more than switching it.

No drink burns belly fat, and you can't target fat loss to one area. Jeera or lemon water is a fine low-calorie start to the morning and helps you drink more water, but the fat comes off through the daily calorie gap you're already running.

Add protein to it: a handful of boiled moong sprouts mixed in, or a bowl of curd on the side, takes it from about 6 g to 15 g protein. Lots of veggies (peas, onion, capsicum) add volume for very few calories.

No, timing matters far less than the day's total: 1800 kcal eaten by 8 pm or by 10 pm does the same thing to your weight. Late eating can be a problem only when it turns into extra snacking, so fruit after dinner is fine if it fits.

Soya chunks are the cheapest by far: about 52 g protein per 100 g dry for a few rupees. After that, roasted chana (about 20 g per 100 g), dal and rajma, curd and milk. A katori of soya sabzi plus a glass of milk a day already adds about 35 g.
Makhana are a good light snack, but not a high-protein one: a bowl of 30 g gives about 3 g protein and 100 kcal. For a protein snack, roasted chana or a bowl of curd does more.

Moong dal chilla stuffed with paneer and capsicum, with a bowl of curd, gives about 30 g protein for 450 kcal. Or tofu or paneer tikka with a bowl of moong dal and one roti, about 35 g for 500 kcal, all without onion, garlic or roots.
